Polygonal Numbers

SequencesAlgebraCounting
Game: See how many dots it takes to build a growing shape with any number of sides.
How to play: Choose the number of sides and the size. Count the dots, and watch which ones each bigger shape adds.

Look for the math

Lay out dots in a triangle, a square, a pentagon, and let the shape grow one row at a time. The counts you get, 1, 3, 6, 10 for triangles and 1, 4, 9, 16 for squares, are the polygonal numbers, studied since the Pythagoreans.

Growing by a gnomon

All the polygons share one corner and the two sides through it. Going from side k − 1 to side k, the two shared sides get one dot longer and the far N − 2 sides are all new: a chain of (N − 2)k + 1 dots, whose two ends are the dots that lengthen the shared sides. Those are the dots drawn in colour. The Greeks called such an L-shaped addition a gnomon.

The formula

Adding up the gnomons from one dot, the n-th N-gonal number (with n dots on a side, so size n − 1 here) is

P(N, n) = (N − 2) · n(n − 1)/2 + n

so it is n plus N − 2 copies of the triangular number T(n − 1). One more side adds one more triangle: P(N, n) = P(N − 1, n) + T(n − 1). The test counted the distinct dots in all 270 pictures the controls allow (3 to 20 sides, size 1 to 15) and every count matched the formula.

Some coincidences

Two triangular numbers in a row make a square: T(n) + T(n + 1) = (n + 1)². Every hexagonal number is also triangular: H(n) = T(2n − 1), so 6, 15, 28 and 45 all appear among 1, 3, 6, 10, 15, 21, 28, 36, 45.

Set 6 sides and size 2, then 3 sides and size 4: both show 15 dots. Can you see the hexagon's dots as a triangle?
